title: GraphQL Operations: A Field Guide to Queries, Mutations, Variables & Fragments
summary: A dense, practical handbook on the GraphQL operation document — how queries and mutations are written, named, parameterized with variables, composed with fragments, and reshaped with aliases. Covers execution semantics, server-side internals, performance trade-offs, and the mistakes that bite real teams.

chapters.title: 1. What an Operation Actually Is
points: A GraphQL request = a document (string) + optional variables map + optional operationName; the document is parsed into an AST before anything runs
Three operation types: query (read, side-effect free by convention), mutation (write), subscription (long-lived event stream)
Anonymous shorthand: `{ user { name } }` is legal only when the document contains exactly ONE operation and it is a query
Named full form: `query GetUser { user { name } }` — keyword + name + selection set
Selection set = the `{ ... }` braces; every non-leaf field MUST have one, every leaf (scalar/enum) MUST NOT
The response shape mirrors the query shape exactly — no surprise fields, no missing fields; this is GraphQL's core promise
Response envelope: `{ "data": {...}, "errors": [...], "extensions": {...} }` — `data` and `errors` can both be present
Executable definitions (operations, fragments) vs type-system definitions (SDL) — a request document may only contain executable definitions
Transport is not part of the spec: HTTP POST with a JSON body is convention, GET with query params works for cacheable reads
The whole document is validated against the schema BEFORE execution; a single invalid field aborts the request with zero resolvers run
Comments use `#` and run to end of line; commas are insignificant whitespace, purely cosmetic
Example minimal request body: `{"query":"query Ping { __typename }","variables":{},"operationName":"Ping"}`
`__typename` is a meta-field available on every object/interface/union — free, no resolver needed, essential for client caches
One document may hold many operations, but exactly one executes per request — selected by operationName

chapters.title: 2. Queries: Reading Data
points: Query root type is usually `type Query` — entry points are its fields, e.g. `user`, `products`, `search`
Fields take arguments: `user(id: "42") { name }` — arguments are named, not positional, and order is irrelevant
Argument types: Int, Float, String, Boolean, ID, enums, input objects, and lists of these; `null` is a legal explicit value
Nesting traverses the graph: `user { posts { comments { author { name } } } }` — one round trip, arbitrary depth
Sibling query fields execute in PARALLEL (spec permits it) since queries are side-effect free
Field-level arguments at any depth: `user { posts(first: 10, orderBy: DATE) { title } }` — not just at the root
Non-null marker `!` in the schema (`String!`) affects error propagation: a null in a non-null field nullifies the parent
List types `[Post!]!` — outer `!` means the list itself is non-null, inner `!` means no null members
Requesting the same field twice with identical args is legal; the result is merged, not duplicated
Cacheable GET form: `GET /graphql?query=...&variables=...&operationName=...` — enables CDN and browser caching
Introspection query `{ __schema { types { name } } }` — how GraphiQL, codegen, and clients learn the schema
Example: `query Feed($n: Int!) { feed(first: $n) { id title author { name } } }`
Deprecated fields still resolve; `@deprecated(reason:)` only surfaces in introspection and tooling warnings
Over-fetching is the client's fault in GraphQL — asking for fields you never render costs real resolver work

chapters.title: 3. Mutations: Writing Data
points: Mutation root type `type Mutation`; syntax is identical to a query — only the keyword and the guarantees differ
CRITICAL: top-level mutation fields execute SERIALLY, in document order, one after the other
Serial execution applies only to the top level — nested selections inside a mutation's payload run in parallel like a query
Two mutations in one document mean the second sees the first's writes — this is a real ordering contract you can rely on
The mutation's return type is the read-back: `updateUser(...) { user { id name } }` — write and re-read in one round trip
Payload-object convention: return `{ user, errors, clientMutationId }` rather than the bare entity, so you can model failure in the type system
Input-object convention (Relay style): a single `input:` argument of an `input` type keeps signatures stable as fields are added
`input` types are distinct from `type` — input types can't have interfaces, unions, or field arguments; they can be recursive
Errors as data vs errors in `errors[]`: a union payload `UpdateResult = User | ValidationError` gives typed, non-nullable error handling
Nothing enforces that mutations write and queries don't — it's convention; putting a write in a query breaks parallelism assumptions
GET must never carry a mutation; keep mutations on POST so caches and prefetchers can't fire them
Example: `mutation Publish($id: ID!) { publishPost(id: $id) { post { id status } errors { field message } } }`
Idempotency: pass a client-generated key so a retried mutation doesn't double-charge
Return the mutated node's `id` and the changed fields so a normalized client cache updates itself with no refetch

chapters.title: 4. Operation Names: Why Anonymous Is a Trap
points: Syntax: `query GetUserProfile { ... }` — the name is an identifier, conventionally PascalCase, unique per document
Required whenever a document holds more than one operation; the request's `operationName` field selects which one runs
Server error if a multi-operation document arrives without `operationName`: "Must provide operation name if query contains multiple operations"
Names appear in server logs, APM traces, and slow-query dashboards — anonymous operations show as an opaque hash or blank
Names key persisted-query allowlists: production servers accept only known operation IDs, blocking arbitrary client queries
Rate limiting and per-operation cost budgets are enforced by name
Codegen derives type names from operation names: `GetUserProfile` yields `GetUserProfileQuery` and `GetUserProfileQueryVariables`
Convention: name = verb + subject, prefix-free (`GetUser`, not `GetUserQuery` — the keyword already says query)
Collisions across files break codegen — most teams enforce globally unique operation names via lint rule
The name has NO effect on the response shape or on execution semantics — it is pure metadata
Anonymous shorthand is fine in GraphiQL and scratch work; it should never ship in application code
eslint-plugin-graphql / graphql-eslint rules: `no-anonymous-operations`, `unique-operation-name`, `naming-convention`
Example of the failure: two anonymous queries in one file silently merged by a bundler produce a runtime error, not a build error
Subscriptions must be named in practice — you need the name to correlate the socket stream with client state

chapters.title: 5. Variables: Parameterizing Operations
points: Declared in the operation signature: `query GetUser($id: ID!) { user(id: $id) { name } }` — `$` prefix, type annotation required
Passed as a separate JSON map: `{"id": "42"}` — never string-interpolated into the document
Why it matters: the document string stays byte-identical across calls, so it parses once, caches, and can be persisted
Security: interpolation invites injection and breaks allowlists; variables are typed and validated by the server
Default values: `query Feed($n: Int = 10)` — used when the variable is omitted or explicitly `null` for a nullable variable
A non-null variable `$id: ID!` may not have a default of `null` and must be supplied on every call
Variable types are limited to input types: scalars, enums, input objects, and lists thereof — never output object types
Variables can be passed into nested field arguments and into directive arguments (`@include(if: $showDetails)`)
Coercion rules: `ID` accepts Int or String, `Int` rejects floats, enums accept unquoted names in the document but quoted strings in the variables JSON
Nullability distinction that trips people: omitting a variable ≠ passing `null` — omitted falls back to the default, `null` is an explicit erase
Unused declared variables are a validation error; undeclared used variables are too
Fragments may reference variables declared by the operation that uses them — the fragment itself cannot declare variables
Example with an input object: `mutation Save($in: PostInput!) { savePost(input: $in) { id } }`, variables `{"in":{"title":"Hi","tags":["a"]}}`
Variables are the unit of cache-key variance for clients: same document + different variables = different cache entry

chapters.title: 6. Fragments: Reusable Selection Sets
points: Definition: `fragment UserFields on User { id name avatarUrl }` — name + `on` + type condition + selection set
Use with the spread operator: `{ user { ...UserFields } }` — spread is inlined during execution, costs nothing extra
The type condition must match the field's type (or be a possible type of its interface/union) or validation fails
Inline fragments (unnamed): `... on Admin { permissions }` — the only way to select type-specific fields on a union
Unions require inline fragments plus `__typename` — you cannot select any common field except `__typename`
Interfaces allow selecting shared fields directly, with inline fragments for the concrete extras
Fragments may spread other fragments; recursion (direct or via a cycle) is a validation error
Colocation pattern: each component declares the fragment for the data it renders; the page query composes them
This is the fix for the classic REST problem — a component's data requirement travels with the component
Fragment names are document-global, must be unique, and every declared fragment must actually be used
Field merging: two spreads selecting `name` produce one `name` in the response; conflicting arguments on the same response key is an error
`@include(if:)` and `@skip(if:)` on a spread give conditional fetching without a second round trip
Relay's `@arguments`/`@argumentDefinitions` add fragment-local variables — a client extension, not core spec
Example: `query Page { viewer { ...Header_user ...Sidebar_user } }` where each fragment lives beside its component

chapters.title: 7. Aliases: Renaming and Repeating Fields
points: Syntax: `alias: field` — `smallPic: avatar(size: 32)` puts the result under the key `smallPic`
Primary purpose: request the SAME field twice with different arguments in one operation
Without aliases this is a validation error — two selections with the same response key and conflicting arguments cannot merge
Example: `{ hero: character(id:"1") { name } villain: character(id:"2") { name } }` — two entities, one round trip
Second purpose: rename server fields to match client-side naming (`user: viewer`, `count: totalRecords`)
Third purpose: resolve name collisions when two fragments on different types both select a differently-typed `status`
The alias becomes the response key; it does NOT change which resolver runs or what arguments are sent
Aliases apply to any field including `__typename` — `kind: __typename` is a common client-cache trick
Batching pattern: alias N copies of a lookup field to fan out one HTTP request into N reads
Anti-pattern: alias-bombing is a DoS vector — 1000 aliased copies of an expensive field multiply server work while looking like one query
Defense: query cost analysis counts aliased duplicates separately; depth limiting alone does not stop it
Aliases are erased in codegen output — the generated TypeScript type uses the alias as its property name
Aliases cannot be used on fragment spreads, only on fields
Field-merging rule of thumb: same response key means the selections must be mergeable; alias when they aren't

chapters.title: 8. Execution Internals: Parse, Validate, Resolve
points: Pipeline: lex → parse to AST → validate against schema → coerce variables → execute → format response
Parsing is pure syntax; a typo like a missing brace fails here with a line/column, before the schema is consulted
Validation runs a list of spec rules: field existence, argument types, fragment type conditions, variable usage, no cycles
Validation is the cacheable expensive step — servers key a validation cache on the document hash, which is why variables matter
Variable coercion happens after validation: JSON values are converted to internal types, failing with a `variables` path error
ExecuteSelectionSet walks the AST breadth-first per level; each field calls its resolver with `(parent, args, context, info)`
`info` carries the field's AST node and path — the hook that lets a resolver see the sub-selection and optimize the query it emits
Default resolver: if none is defined, the executor returns `parent[fieldName]` — most schema fields need no explicit resolver
Resolvers may return promises; the executor awaits them, and sibling fields resolve concurrently in a query

Error propagation: a thrown resolver error becomes `null` for that field and appends to `errors[]` with a `path`; if the field is non-null the null bubbles up to the nearest nullable ancestor, potentially nulling all of `data`
Partial success is normal and correct — `data` with holes plus `errors` is the expected shape, not a bug
The N+1 problem: a list of 100 users each resolving `posts` fires 100 database queries; DataLoader batches them per tick into 1
Directives are executed at collection time: `@skip`/`@include` remove fields before resolvers run, so they cost nothing
Persisted queries: the client sends a hash, the server looks up the document — skips parse and validate, shrinks the request body

chapters.title: 9. Trade-offs, Cost & Comparisons
points: vs REST: one flexible endpoint replaces N rigid ones; you trade HTTP-level caching for client-level normalized caching
Over-fetching solved (ask for exactly your fields); under-fetching solved (nest instead of waterfalling requests)
Cost of flexibility: the server can no longer predict its own workload, so it needs cost analysis and depth limits
Query complexity scoring: assign each field a cost, multiply by list-size arguments, reject over budget before executing
Depth limiting (`maxDepth: 10`) stops cyclic recursion attacks like `friends { friends { friends ... } }`
Alias multiplication and fragment spreads both bypass naive depth limits — cost analysis must count total fields
Pagination trade-off: offset (`skip/take`) is simple but drifts on inserts; cursor/Relay connections are stable but stateless-ugly
Relay Connection spec: `edges { node cursor } pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }` — the industry default shape
Caching comparison — REST: URL-keyed CDN cache; GraphQL: normalized client cache keyed by `__typename` + `id`, plus persisted-query GETs at the edge
Batching comparison — REST: hand-rolled composite endpoints; GraphQL: one document, plus DataLoader for the resolver fan-out
Error comparison — REST: HTTP status codes; GraphQL: HTTP 200 with an `errors[]` array, so status-code-only monitoring goes blind
Versioning comparison — REST: `/v2/`; GraphQL: additive evolution with `@deprecated` and field usage analytics to decide removal
When NOT to use GraphQL: simple CRUD with one consumer, file upload/download heavy APIs, or where HTTP caching is the whole strategy
Client-side cost: normalized caches (Apollo, Relay, urql) are real complexity; fetch + REST is genuinely simpler for small apps

chapters.title: 10. Common Mistakes & Cheat Sheet
points: Mistake: string-interpolating values into the document instead of using variables — kills validation caching and persisted queries
Mistake: shipping anonymous operations — no traces, no allowlist, no codegen types
Mistake: assuming top-level mutations run in parallel — they are serial; assuming nested mutation fields are serial — they are not
Mistake: only checking the HTTP status — a 200 with `errors[]` and partial `data` is the normal failure mode
Mistake: forgetting `__typename` on unions/interfaces, so the client cannot discriminate the returned type
Mistake: marking everything non-null (`!`) — one deep failure then nulls an entire branch or the whole `data`
Mistake: N+1 resolvers with no DataLoader — the query looks cheap, the database sees hundreds of round trips
Mistake: leaving introspection enabled in production with no allowlist — it hands attackers the full attack surface map
Mistake: no depth or cost limit — one recursive query saturates the server
Mistake: omitting a variable when you meant `null` (or vice versa) — omitted uses the default, `null` explicitly clears
Cheat sheet — operation: `query|mutation|subscription Name($var: Type! = default) { ... }`
Cheat sheet — fragment: `fragment F on T { fields }`, spread `...F`, inline `... on T { fields }`
Cheat sheet — alias: `key: field(args)`; directive: `field @include(if: $flag)`
Checklist before shipping an operation: named, variables typed, fragments colocated, `__typename` present, `id` returned on mutation payloads, cost within budget
Mental model to keep: the document is a shape request, variables are the only moving parts, fragments are composition, aliases are the escape hatch for repeats
